chapters.n: Daniel’s story begins around 605 BC, when Babylon’s young king Nebuchadnezzar first moved against Jerusalem. This was the first of several deportations; Ezekiel was taken later, in 597 BC, and the city fell in 586 BC.

f.g: King of Judah about 609–598 BC.
Ruler of Babylon about 605–562 BC; his name is also spelled Nebuchadrezzar.

chapters.n: Daniel stresses that it was the Lord who handed Jehoiakim over—Babylon’s success was not a victory over God. Sacred temple vessels were carried to Babylon (Shinar) and placed in the temple of Nebuchadnezzar’s god as trophies.

f.w: the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand

f.g: An ancient name for the region of Babylonia, where the tower of Babel was built.

f.w: vessels of the house of God

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar orders Ashpenaz, his chief official, to select young men from Judah’s royal family and nobility. Training captive elites was a way to build loyal administrators. Isaiah had foretold that royal descendants would serve in Babylon’s palace.

f.g: Chief court official; the title may simply mean palace officer.

chapters.n: Only the best were chosen: physically flawless, good-looking, intelligent, and well-educated. They would learn the language and literature of the Chaldeans—Babylon’s learned class.

f.g: Here, Babylon’s scholarly class of astrologers and scribes; elsewhere the name of the people.
Skilled, knowledgeable (not sly).
Knowledge, learning.

chapters.n: The students receive food and wine from the king’s own table for a three-year course. Eating the king’s food signaled dependence and loyalty to him.

f.g: Fine food or delicacies from the royal table; “meat” = food in KJV English.

chapters.n: Among the young men from Judah were four friends: Daniel (“God is my judge”), Hananiah (“the Lord is gracious”), Mishael (“who is like God?”), and Azariah (“the Lord has helped”). Each Hebrew name honors the God of Israel.

f.g: Hebrew “God is my judge.”

chapters.n: They are given Babylonian names, many tied to Babylonian gods—an attempt to reshape their identity. Belteshazzar likely means “protect the king’s life,” invoking the god Bel.

f.g: A Babylonian name probably meaning “(Bel) protect his life.”
“Servant of Nego,” likely a play on the god Nabu.

chapters.n: Daniel made a firm decision in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s food and wine. The food may have violated the Law of Moses or been offered to idols. His courage begins with a quiet, private resolve.
God gave Daniel favor and compassion in the official’s eyes. Daniel’s faithfulness is matched by God’s quiet help behind the scenes.

f.w: God had brought Daniel into favour

chapters.n: The official fears that if the young men look unhealthy, the king will blame him—and he could lose his head. His worry is practical, not hostile.

f.g: In worse condition, less healthy-looking.
Risk my life.

chapters.n: Daniel approaches the guard assigned to them. “Melzar” may be a title meaning “guardian” or “steward” rather than a personal name.

f.g: Probably a title—“the steward” or “guardian.”

chapters.n: Daniel proposes a respectful, reasonable test: ten days of simple vegetables and water. He offers a solution rather than a demand.

f.g: Vegetables, legumes, or seeds—simple plant food.
Test.

chapters.n: “Compare us after ten days, then decide.” Daniel trusts God for the results.

f.g: Faces, appearance.

chapters.n: The steward agrees to the trial.
After ten days, the four look healthier and better nourished than those eating the royal food. God honors obedience—echoing the Word of Wisdom’s promise of health.

f.g: Healthier and better nourished.

chapters.n: The steward permanently replaces their royal rations with vegetables.
God gives the four young men knowledge and wisdom, and Daniel receives a special gift: understanding of visions and dreams. That gift sets up the rest of the book.

f.w: Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams

chapters.n: After three years of training, the students are presented to Nebuchadnezzar.
The king interviews them himself, and none compares with these four. They are given positions in the royal court.

f.g: Talked, conversed.
They entered the king’s service.

chapters.n: In every question the king asks, they prove ten times wiser than all his magicians and astrologers. God’s gifts surpass Babylon’s best learning.

f.g: An idiom for “far better.”
Babylon’s experts in omens, dream interpretation, and divination.

chapters.n: Daniel served in Babylon until the first year of Cyrus (about 539 BC), when Persia conquered Babylon—more than sixty years. He outlasted the whole empire that had taken him captive.

f.w: the first year of king Cyrus

chapters.n: Early in his reign, Nebuchadnezzar has disturbing dreams that keep him awake. Ancient kings took dreams seriously as messages from the gods about their rule.

f.w: the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar
f.g: About 603 BC; the date may be counted differently from Daniel 1’s three-year training.
He could not sleep.

chapters.n: The king summons every kind of expert in dreams and omens. Babylon was famous for its libraries of dream interpretation and astrology.

f.g: Those who practiced spells and charms.
Here a class of learned astrologer-priests.

chapters.n: The king says he is troubled and must know what the dream means.
The experts reply in Aramaic, the international language of the day. From here to the end of chapter 7, the book of Daniel itself is written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew.

f.g: Aramaic. Daniel 2:4b–7:28 is written in Aramaic in the original text.
A standard courtly greeting.

chapters.n: The king demands that they tell him both the dream and its meaning, or they will be torn limb from limb and their homes destroyed. “The thing is gone from me” likely means “my decision is firm.”

f.w: The thing is gone from me
f.g: Probably “This is my firm decree,” not “I have forgotten.”
A heap of rubble or refuse.

chapters.n: If they succeed, they will receive gifts, rewards, and honor. The king offers both carrot and stick.
The wise men ask again to hear the dream first.
The king accuses them of stalling, hoping his mood will change.

f.g: You are buying time.

chapters.n: His logic is sharp: if they can truly read the divine meaning, they can also tell him the dream. If they can’t, their interpretations are lies.

f.g: Until circumstances change.

chapters.n: The experts protest that no human being can do this and no king has ever demanded it.
They admit that only the gods could reveal it—and the gods don’t live among mortals. Unknowingly, they set the stage for Daniel to show that his God does reveal secrets to men.

f.w: except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh

chapters.n: Enraged, the king orders all of Babylon’s wise men executed.
Daniel and his friends, now counted among the wise men, are sought out to be killed.
Daniel responds to Arioch, the captain of the king’s guard, with tact and good judgment rather than panic.

f.g: Commander of the king’s bodyguard (literally “chief of the executioners”).

chapters.n: Daniel asks why the decree is so urgent, and Arioch explains the situation.

f.g: Urgent, harsh.

chapters.n: Daniel boldly asks the king for time, promising to give the interpretation—an act of faith before he knows the answer.
Daniel goes home and tells his three friends.
Together they plead with the God of heaven for mercy to reveal the secret. Facing death, their first response is united prayer.

f.w: desire mercies of the God of heaven

f.g: Aramaic raz—a hidden mystery revealed by God.

chapters.n: God reveals the dream to Daniel in a night vision. Daniel’s first act is to praise God.

f.w: Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven

chapters.n: Daniel’s hymn of praise begins: wisdom and power belong to God.
God controls history—He sets up and removes kings and gives wisdom to the wise. This is the theme of the whole book of Daniel.

f.w: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings
he giveth wisdom unto the wise

chapters.n: God reveals hidden things and knows what lies in darkness, because light lives with Him.
Daniel thanks “the God of my fathers” and includes his friends: God has made known what “we” asked. He gives the credit where it belongs.

f.w: O thou God of my fathers

chapters.n: Daniel’s first concern is to save the other wise men—even the pagan astrologers. He asks Arioch to stop the executions and take him to the king.
Arioch hurries Daniel in and takes some credit: “I have found a man.” He calls Daniel one of the captives of Judah.
The king asks Daniel directly whether he can reveal both dream and meaning.
Daniel begins by agreeing that no human expert could do this.

f.g: Diviners or fortune-tellers.

chapters.n: But there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets. Daniel points the king to God and announces that the dream concerns “the latter days.”

f.w: there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets

chapters.n: The king had been lying awake wondering about the future; God answered his very question through the dream.
Daniel insists he is not wiser than anyone else. The revelation came so the king could understand—a model of humility.

f.w: not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have

chapters.n: Daniel describes the dream: a huge, brilliantly shining statue with a terrifying appearance.

f.g: A statue.
Awe-inspiring, frightening.

chapters.n: The statue’s metals decline in value from head to feet: gold, silver, bronze.

f.g: Bronze.

chapters.n: Its legs are iron, and its feet a mix of iron and clay—strong but brittle.
A stone cut out “without hands”—not by any human effort—strikes the statue’s feet and shatters them. The weak point brings the whole thing down.

f.w: a stone was cut out without hands

chapters.n: The whole statue crumbles to dust, blown away like chaff, while the stone grows into a mountain that fills the earth. Latter-day Saints see this as the kingdom of God—the restored Church—rolling forth to fill the earth.

f.g: Husks separated from grain and blown away by the wind.

f.w: became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth

chapters.n: Daniel finishes describing the dream and turns to its meaning. “We” may include his three friends who prayed with him.
Daniel honors Nebuchadnezzar as “king of kings” but reminds him that God gave him his power.

f.g: A title of Babylonian and Persian emperors; ultimately it belongs to Christ.

chapters.n: God made Nebuchadnezzar ruler over people and creatures alike. “Thou art this head of gold”—Babylon is the first kingdom.

f.w: Thou art this head of gold

chapters.n: Two lesser kingdoms will follow. Many interpreters identify silver as the Medo-Persian Empire and bronze as Alexander the Great’s Greek empire.
The fourth kingdom is strong as iron, crushing everything. Many identify it with Rome, though some scholars see it as the Greek kingdoms that followed Alexander.
The fourth kingdom will become divided—strong like iron in some ways, weak like clay in others.

f.g: Mud or wet clay.

chapters.n: Partly strong and partly fragile, the kingdom will lack unity.
Alliances—perhaps through intermarriage—will try to bind the kingdom together, but iron and clay don’t bond.

f.w: they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men
f.g: Possibly royal intermarriages meant to create alliances.
Hold together.

chapters.n: The heart of the dream: during the time of these kings, God will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed or handed to others, and it will stand forever. Latter-day Saints believe this kingdom was restored through Joseph Smith in the last days.

f.w: shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed

chapters.n: The stone cut from the mountain without hands crushes all earthly kingdoms. Daniel declares the dream certain and its interpretation sure.

f.w: the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands

chapters.n: Overwhelmed, the king bows before Daniel and orders offerings and incense. Daniel had pointed him to God, but the pagan king responds in the only way he knows.

f.g: Incense.

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar confesses that Daniel’s God is the God of gods and Lord of kings—a remarkable acknowledgment, though not yet full conversion.

f.w: your God is a God of gods

chapters.n: Daniel is promoted to governor of the province of Babylon and head of all its wise men—echoing Joseph’s rise in Egypt.

f.w: made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon

chapters.n: Daniel does not forget his friends; at his request they are placed over Babylon’s administration. Daniel remains at the king’s court.

f.w: sat in the gate of the king
f.g: Served at the royal court, where officials conducted business.

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar builds a gigantic golden statue—about 90 feet tall and 9 feet wide—on the plain of Dura. Perhaps inspired by his dream’s “head of gold,” he makes the whole image gold, as if his kingdom would never end.

f.g: Sixty cubits—about 90 feet (27 meters); likely gold-plated rather than solid.
A plain in Babylonia; the exact site is uncertain.

chapters.n: Officials from across the empire are summoned to its dedication. The long list of titles stresses the empire’s power and bureaucracy—and the pressure to conform.

f.g: Magistrates or legal officials.

chapters.n: Everyone gathers and stands before the image. The repetition of “the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up” underlines that it is a human creation.
A herald addresses every people, nation, and language—the whole empire.
When the orchestra plays, everyone must bow and worship. Several instrument names are Greek loanwords, reflecting the international culture of the time.

f.g: A triangular stringed instrument (a harp), not the KJV-era trombone.
A stringed instrument like a lyre or zither.
Possibly a bagpipe or a group of instruments playing together.

chapters.n: Refusal means immediate death in a blazing furnace. Furnaces like this were used for firing bricks in Babylon.
At the music, the whole crowd bows. The pressure of the masses is overwhelming.
Some Chaldeans come forward to accuse the Jews—possibly motivated by jealousy over the Jews’ promotion.

f.g: Aramaic idiom, literally “ate the pieces of”—slandered or denounced.

chapters.n: They open with the expected courtly flattery.
They remind the king of his own decree, setting a trap with his words.
They repeat the penalty: the furnace.
The accusation: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego—whom the king himself promoted—ignore him, his gods, and his image. (Daniel is not mentioned; he may have been elsewhere.)

f.g: Have ignored you, paid no attention.

f.w: whom thou hast set over the affairs of the province

chapters.n: The king, furious, summons the three men.
Nebuchadnezzar asks if the report is true, perhaps hoping it isn’t.
He offers them a second chance, then challenges: “Who is the god who can rescue you from my hands?” He has forgotten his own confession in chapter 2.

f.w: who is that God that shall deliver you out of my hands

chapters.n: The three men answer calmly: “We don’t need to defend ourselves.” They feel no need to argue or plead.

f.w: we are not careful to answer thee
f.g: We have no need to answer you; “careful” = anxious.

chapters.n: Their faith is confident: our God is able to deliver us, and He will deliver us from your hand.

f.w: our God whom we serve is able to deliver us

chapters.n: “But if not”—even if God chooses not to save them, they still will not worship the idol. This is faith at its deepest: trusting God regardless of the outcome.
Enraged, the king’s face twists with anger. He orders the furnace heated seven times hotter—as hot as possible.

f.g: Face.
An idiom for “to the maximum.”
Accustomed.

chapters.n: His strongest soldiers tie up the three men to throw them in.
They are bound fully clothed—robes, trousers, and hats—making them seem even more certain to burn.

f.g: Trousers or leggings.

chapters.n: The fire is so hot that the soldiers who throw them in are killed by the flames.
The three men fall, still bound, into the middle of the fire.
The king leaps up in astonishment: “Didn’t we throw three men in, tied up?”

f.g: Astonished.

chapters.n: He sees four men walking freely, unharmed—and the fourth looks like “a son of the gods.” Many Christians, including Latter-day Saints, see a divine presence here, perhaps a preview of Christ standing with His people in their trials.

f.w: the form of the fourth is like the Son of God
f.g: Aramaic “like a son of the gods”—a heavenly being; verse 28 calls him an angel.

chapters.n: The king calls them “servants of the most high God” and invites them out. They walk out of the flames.
The officials gather and see the miracle: not a hair singed, clothes unchanged, not even the smell of smoke. The deliverance is complete.

f.w: nor was an hair of their head singed

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar praises the God who sent His angel. He admires that the men defied the king’s command and risked their lives rather than worship any god but their own.
The king decrees that anyone who insults their God will be torn apart—“there is no other God that can deliver after this sort.” His understanding grows, though he still uses threats.

f.w: there is no other God that can deliver after this sort

chapters.n: The three men are promoted. Their faithfulness under pressure becomes a witness to an empire.
This chapter is written as a royal proclamation from Nebuchadnezzar himself to the whole world—a pagan king’s personal testimony of how God humbled him.

f.g: A standard greeting in royal letters.

chapters.n: The king wants everyone to know the miraculous signs the Most High God has done for him.

f.g: The Most High God.

chapters.n: His praise opens and closes the chapter: God’s kingdom is everlasting. The proud emperor who thought his own kingdom was golden now confesses God’s greater kingdom.

f.w: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom

chapters.n: The story begins at the height of Nebuchadnezzar’s comfort and success—relaxed and prosperous in his palace.

f.g: Literally “green” like a thriving tree—anticipating the dream.

chapters.n: A dream frightens him and disturbs his thoughts.
He calls in all Babylon’s wise men to explain it.
Once again, Babylon’s experts fail—though this time the king tells them the dream.
Finally Daniel comes. The king describes him as having “the spirit of the holy gods”—a pagan way of recognizing God’s Spirit in Daniel.

f.w: the spirit of the holy gods
according to the name of my god
f.g: Belteshazzar contains the name of Bel (Marduk), Babylon’s chief god.

chapters.n: The king calls Daniel “master of the magicians,” his official title, and trusts that no mystery is too hard for him.
In his dream he saw an enormous tree in the center of the earth.

f.w: a tree in the midst of the earth

chapters.n: The tree grows until it reaches the sky and can be seen from the ends of the earth—like the tower of Babel, a symbol of human ambition reaching toward heaven.

f.w: the height thereof reached unto heaven

chapters.n: Its leaves are beautiful and its fruit abundant, feeding and sheltering every creature. A great empire could provide protection and prosperity for many peoples.

f.w: the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof

chapters.n: A “watcher,” a holy one, comes down from heaven. This is an angelic messenger who watches over the earth on God’s behalf.

f.w: a watcher and an holy one
f.g: An angel; Aramaic ʿir, “wakeful one.”

chapters.n: The angel commands that the tree be cut down, its branches lopped, its leaves shaken off, and its fruit scattered. All who relied on it flee.

f.g: Chop down.

chapters.n: But the stump and roots remain, bound with iron and bronze. Partway through, the imagery shifts from a tree to a person living among animals, soaked with dew.

f.w: leave the stump of his roots in the earth
f.g: A sign of hope: the tree can grow back.

chapters.n: His mind will become like an animal’s for “seven times”—probably seven years, or a complete period of time.

f.g: Likely seven years; seven also suggests a full, complete period.

chapters.n: The purpose is clear: so that everyone may know that the Most High rules over human kingdoms and gives them to whomever He chooses—even the lowliest of people.

f.w: the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men

f.g: The humblest or lowliest people.

chapters.n: The king ends his account and asks Daniel to interpret, since only he can.
Daniel is stunned and troubled—he cares about the king and dreads delivering bad news. The king reassures him. Daniel wishes the dream applied to the king’s enemies instead.

f.g: Stunned for a while (“hour” = a short time).

chapters.n: Daniel begins by restating the dream’s image of the great tree.
He repeats its beauty and how it fed and sheltered all creatures.
“It is thou, O king.” Like Nathan telling David “Thou art the man,” Daniel boldly names the king as the tree.
Daniel recounts the angel’s command to cut down the tree but leave its stump.
This is the decree of the Most High, not merely a dream.

The king will be driven from human society, live like an animal, and eat grass like cattle until he acknowledges that God rules. Some historians link this to a rare mental illness in which a person behaves like an animal.

f.w: till thou know that the most High ruleth

chapters.n: The stump means his kingdom will be restored once he learns that heaven rules. Judgment is meant to teach, not just to punish.

f.g: “Heaven” used as a respectful way of referring to God.

chapters.n: Daniel lovingly urges repentance: stop sinning, do what is right, and show mercy to the poor. Perhaps God will delay the judgment. Repentance always opens a door.

f.w: break off thy sins by righteousness

chapters.n: Everything happens just as foretold. The narration now shifts to the third person.
A year passes. God gave the king time to repent.
Walking on his palace roof, Nebuchadnezzar boasts: “Is this not great Babylon, which I built by my power for my glory?” Ancient inscriptions show he did boast of his building projects in Babylon.
Even as he speaks, a voice from heaven declares that his kingdom is taken from him. Pride is answered immediately.

f.w: While the word was in the king's mouth

chapters.n: The voice repeats the sentence: he will live like an animal until he learns who truly rules.
It happens at once. He lives outdoors like an ox, his hair grows like feathers and his nails like claws. The proud king is reduced to the level of an animal.
Back to first person: at the end of the period, the king looks up to heaven—and his sanity returns. Looking up to God is the turning point. He praises the eternal God.

f.w: lifted up mine eyes unto heaven
his kingdom is from generation to generation

chapters.n: All earth’s inhabitants are as nothing compared to God, who does as He wills in heaven and earth. No one can stop Him or demand an explanation.

f.g: The heavenly host—angels or stars.

chapters.n: His reason, honor, and kingdom are restored—with even greater majesty. God restores the humble.

f.w: excellent majesty was added unto me

chapters.n: The king’s final testimony: he praises the King of heaven, whose works are true and whose ways are just—and who can humble the proud. Nebuchadnezzar learned this lesson the hard way.

f.w: those that walk in pride he is able to abase

f.g: Bring low, humble.

chapters.n: About 23 years after Nebuchadnezzar’s death, Belshazzar throws a lavish feast for a thousand nobles. Historical records show he ruled Babylon as co-regent while his father Nabonidus was away; the Persian army was already near the city.

f.g: Son of Nabonidus, Babylon’s last king; he governed Babylon as co-regent around 550–539 BC.

chapters.n: Under the influence of wine, Belshazzar orders the sacred vessels from Jerusalem’s temple brought out for drinking. “Father” can mean ancestor or royal predecessor.

f.g: “Father” in ancient usage could mean predecessor or forebear.
Secondary wives.

chapters.n: The holy vessels used to worship God become party cups. This is deliberate sacrilege—mocking the God of Israel.
While drinking from God’s vessels, they praise idols of every material. The list echoes the metals of Nebuchadnezzar’s statue in chapter 2.

f.w: praised the gods of gold, and of silver

chapters.n: Suddenly the fingers of a human hand appear and write on the plaster wall near the lampstand, where the light is brightest. Archaeologists have found Babylon’s palace walls coated in white plaster.

f.g: Lampstand.

chapters.n: The king turns pale, terrified; his legs give way and his knees knock together. The party is over.

f.w: the joints of his loins were loosed
f.g: His legs gave out from fear.

chapters.n: The king offers rich rewards to anyone who can read it: royal purple (scarlet), a gold chain, and the rank of third ruler. Third, because Nabonidus was first and Belshazzar second.

f.g: Purple—a color reserved for royalty and high officials.

f.w: the third ruler in the kingdom
f.g: Fits the history: Nabonidus and Belshazzar ruled first and second.

chapters.n: The wise men can’t read it or explain it.
The king’s terror grows, and his nobles are bewildered.

f.g: Astonished, perplexed.

chapters.n: The queen—probably the queen mother, perhaps Nebuchadnezzar’s widow or daughter—comes in, having heard the commotion. She calmly reassures the king.

f.g: Likely the queen mother, since the king’s wives were already at the feast.

chapters.n: She remembers a man with the spirit of the holy gods, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made chief of the wise men. Daniel had apparently been forgotten by the new regime.
She praises Daniel’s gifts: he explains dreams, solves riddles, and unravels hard problems.

f.g: Riddles, puzzling sayings.
Literally “untying knots”—solving hard problems.

chapters.n: Daniel, now about 80 years old, is brought in. The king identifies him somewhat condescendingly as one of the exiles from Judah.

f.g: Judah.

chapters.n: Belshazzar repeats what he has heard about Daniel’s wisdom.
He admits that his wise men failed.
He offers Daniel the same rich rewards.
Daniel politely declines the rewards—keep your gifts—but agrees to read the writing. God’s message is not for sale.

f.w: Let thy gifts be to thyself

chapters.n: Before interpreting, Daniel gives a history lesson: the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar his kingdom and glory.
Nebuchadnezzar’s power was absolute—he could kill or spare, promote or demote whomever he wished.
But when he became proud, God removed him from his throne and stripped his glory.
Daniel recalls Nebuchadnezzar’s humiliation among the animals until he learned that God rules over human kingdoms.

f.g: Wild donkeys.

f.w: the most high God ruled in the kingdom of men

chapters.n: The heart of the charge: “You knew all this, and still did not humble yourself.” Sinning against knowledge is especially serious.
Belshazzar has defied the Lord of heaven by profaning His vessels and praising lifeless idols—while ignoring the God who holds his very breath and controls all his ways.

f.w: which see not, nor hear, nor know
the God in whose hand thy breath is

chapters.n: That is why God sent the hand and the writing.
The inscription reads: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. These are Aramaic words for weights or coins—a mina, a shekel, and half-minas—and they also carry verbal meanings.

f.g: Units of weight/money: mina, shekel, and half-shekels (“u-” = and). Daniel reads them as verbs.

chapters.n: MENE means “numbered”: God has counted the days of your kingdom and brought it to an end.

f.g: From a root meaning “to count” or “number.”

chapters.n: TEKEL means “weighed”: you have been weighed on God’s scales and found too light—lacking in moral worth.

f.w: Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting

f.g: Lacking, deficient.

chapters.n: PERES (singular of PARSIN) means “divided,” and sounds like “Paras,” Persia. Your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.

f.g: “Divided,” with a wordplay on Persia (Paras).

chapters.n: Belshazzar keeps his word and honors Daniel—but the honor will last only a few hours.
That same night, Belshazzar is killed. Ancient historians record that the Persians took Babylon in 539 BC, some saying it happened during a festival.

f.w: In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain

chapters.n: “Darius the Mede” takes over at about 62 years old. He is not yet identified in other ancient records; scholars suggest he may be another name for Cyrus or for a governor such as Gubaru.

f.g: Not clearly identified outside Daniel; possibly a governor under Cyrus or a title for Cyrus himself.

chapters.n: Under the new Persian rule, Darius organizes the empire with 120 regional officials. The Persians were known for this kind of efficient administration.

f.g: Satraps—provincial governors.

chapters.n: Three senior administrators oversee the governors to protect the king’s interests, and Daniel is one of them—now an elderly statesman.

f.g: Chief administrators or commissioners.

f.w: the king should have no damage
f.g: So the king would suffer no loss (from corruption or mismanagement).

chapters.n: Daniel stands out because of his “excellent spirit,” and the king plans to put him over the whole kingdom—like Joseph in Egypt.

f.w: an excellent spirit was in him

f.g: Distinguished himself; excelled.

chapters.n: Jealous rivals dig for scandal but find nothing: Daniel is honest, faithful, and careful. His integrity is airtight.

f.w: they could find none occasion nor fault

f.g: Grounds for an accusation.

chapters.n: They realize the only way to trap Daniel is through his devotion to God. His faith is his only “weakness” in their eyes.
The conspirators come as a crowd to the king—the Aramaic suggests they came in a throng, perhaps to pressure him.

f.g: Came thronging; acted in concert.

chapters.n: They falsely claim “all” the officials agree (Daniel obviously didn’t). They propose that for thirty days no one may pray to any god or man except the king, under penalty of the lions’ den.

f.g: Ancient Near Eastern kings kept lions in captivity, sometimes for royal hunts.

chapters.n: They urge him to make it irrevocable under Persian law, which—once sealed by the king—could not be changed.

f.w: the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not

chapters.n: Flattered, Darius signs the decree without seeing the trap.

Daniel knows the law is signed, yet goes home and prays as always—kneeling three times a day by windows open toward Jerusalem, giving thanks. He neither hides nor makes a show; he simply keeps doing what is right.

f.w: his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem

chapters.n: The conspirators rush in and catch Daniel praying and pleading with God.

f.g: Humble, earnest request.

chapters.n: They first get the king to confirm the unchangeable decree before naming their target.
Then they accuse Daniel, sneering at him as an exile from Judah who ignores the king.

f.g: Pays no attention to you.

chapters.n: The king is furious—with himself. He realizes he has been manipulated and works until sunset trying to find a legal way to save Daniel.

f.g: Deeply distressed.

chapters.n: The conspirators return to press the point: Persian law cannot be changed. The king is trapped by his own decree.
Daniel is thrown into the den. The king says, perhaps as a hopeful wish: “Your God, whom you serve continually, will deliver you.”

f.w: Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee

chapters.n: A stone seals the den, stamped with the king’s and nobles’ signet rings so no one can tamper with it. Many readers see a parallel to the sealed tomb of Jesus.

f.g: A seal ring pressed into clay or wax as an official signature.

f.w: a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den

chapters.n: The king spends a sleepless night fasting, refusing entertainment—his anxiety shows how much he cares for Daniel.

f.g: The Aramaic word is uncertain—perhaps entertainment or concubines.

chapters.n: At first light he hurries to the den.
With anguish he calls out: “Daniel, servant of the living God, was your God able to deliver you?” The phrase “the living God” contrasts with lifeless idols.

f.g: Anguished, sorrowful.

chapters.n: Daniel answers with a respectful greeting—he is alive!
God sent His angel to shut the lions’ mouths. Daniel affirms his innocence before God and his loyalty to the king—he was faithful to both.

f.w: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths

f.g: Innocence, blamelessness.

chapters.n: Daniel is lifted out without a scratch “because he believed in his God.” Faith is named as the key.

f.w: because he believed in his God

chapters.n: The accusers and their families are thrown to the lions, which overpower them before they hit the bottom. This harsh punishment reflects Persian practice, not God’s command; it shows the trap turned back on those who set it.

f.w: the lions had the mastery of them

f.g: Before.

chapters.n: Darius issues a proclamation to all nations, much like Nebuchadnezzar’s in chapter 4.
He commands everyone to revere Daniel’s God—the living, eternal God whose kingdom will never be destroyed. Another pagan king testifies of God’s everlasting kingdom.

f.w: his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed

chapters.n: God delivers, rescues, and works wonders—as He showed by saving Daniel from the lions.
Daniel prospers under Darius and Cyrus. Some scholars read this as “Darius, that is, Cyrus the Persian,” suggesting they may be the same person.
The book now shifts from stories about Daniel to visions Daniel received. This one comes in Belshazzar’s first year (about 553 BC), before the events of chapter 5. Daniel writes down the main points.

f.g: About 553 BC, when Belshazzar began ruling Babylon for his father.

f.w: told the sum of the matters
f.g: Recorded the essentials.

chapters.n: Winds from every direction churn up the great sea. In ancient imagery, the sea stood for chaos and the restless nations of the world.

f.g: The stormy sea—a symbol of chaotic nations.

chapters.n: Four great beasts rise from the sea, each different. Like the statue of chapter 2, they represent four successive empires—but now seen as God sees them: as predatory beasts.
The first is a lion with eagle’s wings—Babylon. Winged lions decorated Babylon’s palaces. Its wings are plucked and it is given a human heart, recalling Nebuchadnezzar’s humbling and restoration.

f.w: like a lion, and had eagle's wings
a man's heart was given to it

chapters.n: The second beast is a bear raised on one side, with three ribs in its mouth—commonly identified with Medo-Persia, where the Persians dominated the Medes. The ribs may be conquered nations.

f.w: it raised up itself on one side
f.g: Possibly the stronger Persian side of the Medo-Persian alliance.

chapters.n: The third is a leopard with four wings and four heads—swift conquest. Many link it to Alexander the Great’s rapid conquests and the empire’s later division among four generals.
The fourth beast is unlike any animal—terrifying, iron-toothed, crushing everything. It matches the iron legs of the statue in chapter 2. It has ten horns, symbols of power.
A small horn rises, uprooting three others. It has human eyes and a boastful mouth—a proud ruler who sets himself against God.

The scene shifts to heaven. Thrones are set up and the Ancient of Days takes His seat, clothed in white, hair like pure wool, on a fiery throne with burning wheels. Latter-day Saint scripture identifies the Ancient of Days as Adam, who will preside at a great gathering before the Second Coming.

f.g: The thrones were placed (set up), not overthrown.

chapters.n: A river of fire flows from before Him, and countless beings serve Him. The court sits and books are opened—records by which all will be judged.
Daniel keeps watching because of the horn’s boasting—until the fourth beast is killed and burned. Pride meets judgment.
The other beasts lose their power but are allowed to live for a while. God sets the limits of every empire.

f.g: For a set period.

chapters.n: One “like the Son of man”—a human figure, in contrast to the beasts—comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days. Jesus took “Son of Man” as His favorite title for Himself, and Latter-day Saints understand this as Christ receiving the kingdom.

f.w: one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven

chapters.n: He receives everlasting dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples will serve. Unlike the beastly empires, His kingdom will never pass away—the “stone” of chapter 2.

f.w: his dominion is an everlasting dominion

chapters.n: Daniel is deeply disturbed by what he has seen.

f.w: in the midst of my body
f.g: Literally “in its sheath”—his spirit within his body.

chapters.n: He asks one of the heavenly attendants what it all means, and is given the interpretation.

f.w: one of them that stood by
f.g: An angel among the heavenly court.

chapters.n: The four beasts are four kings (or kingdoms) that rise from the earth.
But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever. “Saints” means God’s holy, covenant people—the same word Latter-day Saints use for themselves.

f.w: the saints of the most High shall take the kingdom

f.g: Holy ones—God’s covenant people.

chapters.n: Daniel wants to know more about the fourth beast—with iron teeth and bronze claws, crushing everything.
He asks also about the ten horns and the arrogant little horn that overthrew three and looked more imposing than the rest.

f.g: More imposing than the others.

chapters.n: That horn wages war against the saints and seems to win.

f.w: made war with the saints, and prevailed against them

chapters.n: Its success lasts only until the Ancient of Days comes, judgment is given in favor of the saints, and they possess the kingdom. Evil’s victories are temporary.

f.w: judgment was given to the saints

chapters.n: The angel explains: the fourth beast is a fourth kingdom, different from all others, that will devour the whole earth.
The ten horns are ten kings from that kingdom. Another will arise after them, different, and will bring down three kings.

This ruler will speak against God, oppress the saints, and try to change sacred times and laws—for “a time, times, and half a time” (often read as three and a half years). Many link this first to Antiochus IV, and Latter-day Saints also see a pattern of apostasy and opposition to God’s kingdom.

f.w: a time and times and the dividing of time
f.g: Probably 1 + 2 + ½ = 3½ “times”—a limited period of persecution.

f.w: think to change times and laws

chapters.n: But the heavenly court will sit, take away his power, and destroy it completely.
Then the kingdom—all the greatness of every kingdom under heaven—will be given to the saints, under God’s everlasting rule.

f.w: shall be given to the people of the saints of the most High

chapters.n: The vision ends. Daniel is shaken and pale, but he keeps the matter in his heart, pondering it—as Mary later pondered things in her heart.

f.w: I kept the matter in my heart

f.g: Thoughts.

chapters.n: Two years after the vision of the four beasts, Daniel receives another. From this chapter to the end, the book returns to Hebrew. This vision zooms in on the second and third kingdoms of chapter 7.

f.w: the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar
f.g: About 551 BC. Daniel 8–12 is written in Hebrew.

f.w: that which appeared unto me at the first

chapters.n: In vision Daniel finds himself at Shushan (Susa), a royal city in Elam that would become a Persian capital, beside the Ulai canal.

f.g: Susa, later a capital of the Persian Empire.
A region east of Babylon, in modern southwestern Iran.

chapters.n: A ram with two horns, one taller than the other, which grew up last—Media and Persia, with Persia becoming dominant later.

f.w: a ram which had two horns

chapters.n: The ram charges west, north, and south, and no one can stop it. The Persian Empire expanded in all these directions.
A male goat from the west races across the earth so fast its feet don’t touch the ground. It has one prominent horn between its eyes—Alexander the Great.

f.g: A male goat.
A conspicuous, prominent horn.

chapters.n: The goat charges the ram in furious power.
It strikes the ram, shatters both horns, and tramples it. Alexander defeated the Persian Empire in a series of battles from 334 to 331 BC.

f.g: Rage, fury.

chapters.n: At the height of its power, the great horn breaks, and four horns grow in its place. Alexander died suddenly in 323 BC, and his empire was split among four of his generals.

f.g: Grew.

chapters.n: From one of these comes a “little horn” that grows toward the south, east, and “the pleasant land”—Israel. Most scholars identify this ruler with Antiochus IV Epiphanes of the Seleucid kingdom (175–164 BC).

f.g: The beautiful land—the land of Israel.

chapters.n: It grows so arrogant that it attacks the host of heaven, throwing some stars down and trampling them—probably God’s faithful people, pictured as stars.
It even challenges the Prince of the host—God Himself—stopping the daily sacrifice and defiling the sanctuary. Antiochus did ban temple sacrifices in Jerusalem in 167 BC.

f.g: The continual morning and evening offerings.
Exalted himself, acted with arrogance.

chapters.n: Because of transgression, the horn is allowed to overpower the sacrifice and throw truth to the ground. For a time, evil seems to prosper.

f.g: Did as it pleased and succeeded.

chapters.n: Daniel hears two holy ones asking, “How long will this desecration last?” It is the cry of the suffering faithful in every age.

f.g: Holy one—an angel.
The sin that causes horror and ruin.

chapters.n: The answer: 2,300 “evenings and mornings,” then the sanctuary will be restored. This may mean 1,150 days (counting evening and morning sacrifices) or 2,300 days. The Maccabees rededicated the temple in 164 BC—the origin of Hanukkah.

f.w: two thousand and three hundred days
f.g: Literally “evening-morning” 2,300—possibly 1,150 days of missed sacrifices.

f.w: then shall the sanctuary be cleansed
f.g: Restored to its right condition.

chapters.n: As Daniel seeks understanding, someone who looks like a man appears before him.
A voice calls from the Ulai: “Gabriel, explain the vision to this man.” This is the first time an angel is named in the Bible. Latter-day Saints understand Gabriel to be Noah.

f.g: Hebrew “God is my strength” (or “man of God”).

chapters.n: Daniel falls on his face in fear. Gabriel calls him “son of man” (mortal) and says the vision concerns “the time of the end.”
Daniel collapses into a deep stupor, but the angel touches him and raises him to his feet.

f.w: he touched me, and set me upright

chapters.n: Gabriel will explain what happens at the end of the period of wrath—at the time God has appointed.

f.g: The period of God’s wrath or of persecution.

chapters.n: The two-horned ram is the kings of Media and Persia.
The goat is the king of Greece; the great horn is its first king—Alexander.

f.g: Greece (Hebrew Yavan).

chapters.n: The four horns are four kingdoms that arise from his empire, but none as powerful as he was.
Late in their rule, when wickedness reaches its full measure, a fierce king skilled in intrigue will arise.

f.g: Skilled in riddles, intrigue, or deceit.

f.w: when the transgressors are come to the full

chapters.n: His power will be great, but not his own—permitted by God. He will cause astonishing destruction and persecute God’s holy people.
Through cunning he will make deceit prosper, exalt himself, and destroy many who feel safe. He will even oppose the Prince of princes—but he will be broken “without hand,” by God, not by human power.

f.g: God; Christians see Christ as Prince of princes.

f.w: he shall be broken without hand

f.g: Cunning, shrewdness.

chapters.n: The vision of the evenings and mornings is true. Daniel must “shut up” (seal and preserve) it, because it concerns the distant future.
Daniel is exhausted and ill for days. Then he gets up and returns to the king’s business—faithful in daily duties even while bewildered by what he saw.

f.w: I Daniel fainted, and was sick certain days

chapters.n: The setting is the first year of Darius the Mede, right after Babylon fell to the Persians (about 539–538 BC). A new era had begun, and Daniel wondered what it meant for his people.

f.g: The Babylonians.

chapters.n: Studying the scriptures—Jeremiah’s prophecy—Daniel realized the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation were nearly complete. Even a great prophet learns by searching the written word.

f.g: Counted roughly from the first deportation (605 BC) to the return under Cyrus (538 BC).

chapters.n: Rather than simply waiting, Daniel turns to God with prayer, fasting, sackcloth, and ashes—signs of humility and mourning.

f.g: Rough goat-hair cloth and ashes, worn as signs of grief and repentance.
I turned my full attention.

chapters.n: Daniel’s prayer begins with praise: God is great and awe-inspiring, and keeps His covenant and steadfast love toward those who love and obey Him.

f.g: Awe-inspiring.

chapters.n: Daniel, though personally righteous, says “we have sinned.” He identifies with his people rather than standing apart from them—a model of intercessory prayer.
Israel ignored the prophets God sent to every level of society—kings, leaders, and ordinary people.

f.w: Neither have we hearkened unto thy servants the prophets

chapters.n: God is righteous; Israel deserves the shame they now feel. “Confusion of faces” means open shame. Israel is scattered both near and far.

f.g: Public shame, embarrassment.

chapters.n: Shame belongs to every level of the nation—kings, princes, and ancestors—because all sinned.
Yet mercy and forgiveness belong to God. Daniel holds both truths together: our guilt and God’s grace.

f.w: To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses

chapters.n: Israel did not obey the laws God gave through His prophets.
The curses written in the Law of Moses have come upon them because of their disobedience, just as Moses warned.

f.w: the curse is poured upon us

chapters.n: God fulfilled His warnings. Nothing anywhere has matched the disaster that struck Jerusalem.

f.w: under the whole heaven hath not been done

chapters.n: Even after disaster struck, Israel still did not seek God or turn from sin. Suffering alone doesn’t produce repentance.

f.w: yet made we not our prayer before the LORD

chapters.n: God “watched over” the calamity and brought it, because He is just in all He does.

f.g: Kept the threatened disaster ready and carried it out.

chapters.n: Daniel appeals to history: the God who rescued Israel from Egypt can rescue them again. Past deliverance is a basis for present hope.

f.w: brought thy people forth out of the land of Egypt

chapters.n: He pleads for God to turn His anger from Jerusalem, His holy mountain, which has become a laughingstock to the nations.

f.g: Mount Zion, the temple mount.

chapters.n: “Make your face shine on your desolate sanctuary”—echoing the priestly blessing. Daniel asks for God’s favor to return to the ruined temple.
Daniel asks God to listen and look—not because Israel deserves it, but because of His great mercy. The whole prayer rests on grace.
The prayer climaxes with urgent, short cries: Lord, hear! Lord, forgive! Lord, act! Don’t delay—for the sake of Your own name and people.

f.w: O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive

f.g: Do not delay.

chapters.n: While Daniel is still praying and confessing—both his own sin and his people’s—the answer comes.
Gabriel, the angel from the earlier vision, arrives swiftly at the time of the evening offering. Though the temple lay in ruins, Daniel still kept its sacred times of prayer.

f.g: The time of the evening sacrifice, about 3 p.m.

chapters.n: Gabriel says he has come to give Daniel insight and understanding.
The answer was sent the moment Daniel began praying, because he is “greatly beloved” by God. Heaven responds to sincere prayer immediately, even if the answer takes time to arrive.

f.w: At the beginning of thy supplications

chapters.n: “Seventy weeks” (seventy “sevens,” probably 490 years) are decreed for Israel and Jerusalem—to end sin, make atonement, bring everlasting righteousness, fulfill prophecy, and anoint the Most Holy. Christians see these purposes fulfilled through Jesus Christ’s atonement.

f.g: Hebrew “seventy sevens”—usually read as 490 years.
Hebrew kipper—to make atonement.
To anoint a most holy place—or, many Christians read, the Most Holy One.

chapters.n: From the command to rebuild Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed ruler will be “seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.” Jerusalem will be rebuilt in difficult times—fulfilled in the days of Ezra and Nehemiah.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ nagid—“an anointed one, a ruler.”

f.w: the street shall be built again, and the wall

chapters.n: After the sixty-two weeks, “Messiah shall be cut off, but not for himself”—Christians see Christ’s death on behalf of others. A coming ruler’s people will destroy the city and sanctuary, fulfilled when Rome destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.

f.w: shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself
shall destroy the city and the sanctuary

chapters.n: During the final “week,” a covenant is made, and in the middle of it sacrifices stop. An “abomination of desolation” defiles the temple until the decreed end. Jesus referred to this prophecy in His teachings about Jerusalem’s fall and the last days.

f.g: Often rendered “the abomination that makes desolate.”
The decreed end.

chapters.n: Daniel’s final vision (chapters 10–12) comes in the third year of Cyrus, about 536 BC. By now some Jews had returned to Jerusalem, but Daniel, now very old, remained in Persia. The message was true but concerned a long, hard conflict.

f.w: the third year of Cyrus king of Persia

f.g: Or “it concerned a great conflict (or hardship).”

chapters.n: Daniel had been mourning for three full weeks—perhaps grieving over troubles facing the returned exiles, whose temple rebuilding met opposition.
He fasted partially—no rich food, meat, or wine—and did not use the scented oils normally applied to the skin. His fast showed earnest seeking.

f.g: Rich or delicious food.
Using olive oil on the skin was a daily comfort; skipping it was a sign of mourning.

chapters.n: On the 24th day of the first month—just after Passover—Daniel is by the Tigris River.

f.g: The Tigris River.

chapters.n: He sees a man in linen with a belt of fine gold. Linen was worn by priests and heavenly messengers.

f.g: A place known for fine gold; location uncertain.

chapters.n: His body gleams like a gemstone, his face like lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his limbs like polished bronze, and his voice like a roaring crowd. John’s vision of the resurrected Christ in Revelation is strikingly similar.

f.g: A precious stone, possibly yellow chrysolite or topaz.

f.w: his eyes as lamps of fire

chapters.n: Only Daniel sees the vision. His companions feel terror and run to hide—like Paul’s companions on the road to Damascus.

f.w: the men that were with me saw not the vision

chapters.n: Left alone, Daniel loses all strength; his healthy color drains away. Encountering heavenly glory is physically overwhelming for mortals.

f.w: my comeliness was turned in me into corruption
f.g: My healthy appearance turned deathly pale.

f.w: there remained no strength in me

chapters.n: At the sound of the voice, Daniel falls face-down into a deep stupor.

f.w: in a deep sleep on my face

chapters.n: A hand touches him and lifts him, trembling, onto his hands and knees.
The messenger calls him “greatly beloved,” tells him to stand, and explains that he has been sent to him. Daniel stands, trembling.
“Fear not.” From the very first day Daniel humbled himself to seek understanding, his prayer was heard. The messenger came because of his prayer.

f.g: Prayer is heard at once, even if the answer is delayed.
To humble yourself, as by fasting.

chapters.n: The delay had a cause: a spiritual opponent, “the prince of the kingdom of Persia,” resisted for 21 days—the same length as Daniel’s fast—until Michael came to help. This verse lifts the curtain on unseen spiritual conflict behind earthly events.

f.w: the prince of the kingdom of Persia
f.g: A spiritual power influencing Persia—not the human king.

f.w: Michael, one of the chief princes
f.g: Latter-day Saint scripture identifies Michael the archangel as Adam.

chapters.n: The messenger has come to explain what will happen to Daniel’s people in the latter days—a vision reaching far into the future.
Overcome again, Daniel bows his face to the ground and can’t speak.

f.g: I was unable to speak.

chapters.n: Someone in human likeness touches his lips, and he can speak again. He explains that the vision has filled him with anguish and drained his strength.

f.w: my sorrows are turned upon me
f.g: Pangs of distress, like labor pains, have gripped me.

chapters.n: “How can someone like me talk with someone like you?” He has no strength and can barely breathe.
Again the human-like figure touches him and gives him strength.
“Don’t be afraid, greatly beloved. Peace. Be strong—be strong!” As the words are spoken, strength comes. God’s word itself empowers.

f.w: peace be unto thee, be strong

chapters.n: The messenger must return to fight the prince of Persia, and afterward the prince of Greece will come—another empire with its own spiritual powers behind it.

f.g: The spiritual power behind Greece, the kingdom to follow Persia.

chapters.n: He will reveal what is written in “the book of truth”—God’s record of the future. Only Michael, Israel’s guardian prince, stands with him in this conflict.

f.g: God’s book of decrees—His record of what will happen.

chapters.n: The messenger continues from chapter 10, mentioning that he had strengthened Darius the Mede (or Michael) in that king’s first year. Behind earthly thrones, heavenly helpers are at work.

f.w: stood to confirm and to strengthen him
f.g: “Him” may be Darius or Michael (Daniel 10:21).

chapters.n: This chapter is the most detailed prophecy in the Old Testament. Three more Persian kings will come, then a fourth, very rich, who will provoke Greece. Many identify him with Xerxes I, who invaded Greece in 480 BC.

f.w: the fourth shall be far richer than they all
f.g: Commonly identified as Xerxes I (Ahasuerus of Esther).
Greece.

chapters.n: A mighty king will rise and do whatever he wants—Alexander the Great (336–323 BC).
At his height his empire breaks into four parts, not passed to his heirs. Alexander’s young sons were killed, and his generals divided the empire.

f.w: divided toward the four winds of heaven

chapters.n: From here on, “the king of the south” means Egypt’s Ptolemaic rulers and “the king of the north” the Seleucid rulers of Syria. Israel lay between them. Ptolemy I was strong, but one of his former officers, Seleucus I, grew even stronger.

f.g: The Ptolemies, Greek kings of Egypt.
Probably Seleucus I, once Ptolemy’s officer, who founded the northern (Seleucid) kingdom.

chapters.n: Years later, a peace treaty is sealed by marriage: Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, married the Seleucid king Antiochus II. The alliance failed—she, her child, and her attendants were murdered.

f.w: the king's daughter of the south
f.g: Berenice, married to Antiochus II about 252 BC.

f.w: she shall not retain the power of the arm
f.g: She will not keep her influence.

chapters.n: Her brother, “a branch from her roots”—Ptolemy III—avenged her by invading the northern kingdom and winning.

f.g: A relative—her brother Ptolemy III.
In his place, as successor.

chapters.n: He carried back to Egypt captured idols, officials, and treasures of silver and gold, and outlived the northern king.
The northern king (Seleucus II) tried a counterattack on Egypt but was forced to return home.
The northern king’s sons gathered great armies. One of them, Antiochus III (“the Great”), swept south like a flood toward Egypt’s fortress.

f.g: Sweep through like a flood.

chapters.n: The furious southern king (Ptolemy IV) fought back. At the battle of Raphia (217 BC) he defeated Antiochus III’s huge army.

f.g: Anger, rage.

chapters.n: Victory made the southern king proud, and he killed tens of thousands—but he did not follow up his advantage.
Years later the northern king returned with an even larger, richer army.
Many rose against the south, including some violent men among the Jews who tried to fulfill prophecy by force—but they failed.

f.g: Violent men among your own people.
Trying to bring a prophecy to pass by their own efforts.

chapters.n: The northern king besieged and took a fortified city—likely Sidon, after Antiochus III won the battle of Panium (about 200 BC). Egypt’s best troops couldn’t stop him.

f.g: Build a siege ramp.
A well-fortified city.

chapters.n: Now unopposed, he took control of “the glorious land”—Judea passed from Egyptian to Seleucid rule around 198 BC.

f.g: The beautiful land—Israel.

chapters.n: He tried to gain Egypt through marriage, giving his daughter (Cleopatra I) to young Ptolemy V. But she sided with her husband and Egypt rather than her father.

f.g: A young woman—his daughter Cleopatra I.

chapters.n: He turned to the coastlands of Asia Minor and Greece, but a commander—the Roman Lucius Scipio—stopped him at Magnesia (190 BC), turning his insolence back on him.

f.g: Coastlands—Asia Minor and the Greek islands.
Insolence, scorn.

chapters.n: He retreated to his own fortresses, then stumbled and fell. Antiochus III died in 187 BC while trying to plunder a temple in Elymais to pay his debts to Rome.
His successor (Seleucus IV) sent a tax collector—traditionally Heliodorus—to raise funds, even from the Jerusalem temple. He reigned briefly and was assassinated, not in battle.

f.g: One who sends out a tax collector.
Possibly the temple in Jerusalem, the kingdom’s glory.

chapters.n: Next comes a “contemptible person” who wasn’t the rightful heir but took the throne through intrigue and flattery: Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC), the “little horn” of chapter 8.

f.g: A despicable man—Antiochus IV, who called himself Epiphanes (“God manifest”).

chapters.n: Opposing armies are swept away before him, and even “the prince of the covenant” is broken—probably the high priest Onias III, who was removed and later murdered.

f.g: Probably the high priest Onias III.

chapters.n: He makes alliances and then breaks them through deceit, rising to power with only a small following.

f.g: Alliance, treaty.

chapters.n: He invades rich provinces and lavishly distributes plunder to buy loyalty—something his predecessors hadn’t done. He plots against fortresses, but only for a time; God sets the limit.

f.g: Devise plans, plot.
Only for a limited time.

chapters.n: He launches a great army against Egypt (170–169 BC). The southern king (Ptolemy VI) fights back but is defeated, partly through plots against him.
Ptolemy’s own advisers—those who ate at his table—betray him, and his army is overwhelmed.

f.w: they that feed of the portion of his meat
f.g: Those who eat at his table—his trusted advisers.

chapters.n: The two kings sit at one table, lying to each other with evil intent, but neither succeeds—the outcome is in God’s hands at the appointed time.

f.w: they shall speak lies at one table
f.g: Antiochus IV and his nephew Ptolemy VI negotiated with mutual deceit.

chapters.n: Returning home rich, Antiochus turns against the holy covenant. In 169 BC he plundered the Jerusalem temple.

f.w: his heart shall be against the holy covenant
f.g: Hostile to the Jews’ religion and covenant with God.

chapters.n: He invades Egypt again (168 BC), but this time the outcome is different.

Ships from Kittim—Romans—confront him. A Roman envoy famously drew a circle in the sand and ordered him to decide before stepping out of it; humiliated, Antiochus withdrew and vented his rage on the Jews, favoring those who abandoned the covenant.

f.g: Kittim—originally Cyprus, later used for western powers such as Rome.

f.w: have intelligence with them that forsake the holy covenant
f.g: Show favor to Jews who abandoned their faith.

chapters.n: His forces desecrate the temple, stop the daily sacrifice, and set up “the abomination that makes desolate”—in 167 BC an altar to Zeus was placed on the temple altar. Jesus later spoke of a future “abomination of desolation.”

f.g: The temple fortress.

chapters.n: He seduces covenant-breakers with flattery, but those who know their God stand firm and act boldly—like the Maccabees who resisted. Knowing God gives strength.

f.w: the people that do know their God shall be strong

f.g: Act with courage and effect.

chapters.n: The wise among the people will teach many, yet some will suffer martyrdom—by sword, fire, captivity, and plunder.

f.g: The wise or insightful (Hebrew maskilim).

f.w: they shall fall by the sword

chapters.n: When they fall, they will receive a little help—perhaps the Maccabean revolt—while some join them insincerely.

f.g: Helped.

chapters.n: Some of the wise will die, but their trials will refine, purify, and make them white—until the appointed end. Suffering for faith can purify the faithful.

f.w: to try them, and to purge, and to make them white

chapters.n: The king exalts himself above every god and blasphemes the God of gods, prospering only until God’s wrath runs its course. Antiochus fits this description, and many readers also see a pattern of a future anti-God figure.

f.g: Astonishing blasphemies.

chapters.n: He disregards his ancestors’ gods and “the one desired by women” (perhaps a popular god such as Tammuz), placing himself above all.

f.g: Possibly a deity popular with women, such as Tammuz or Adonis.

chapters.n: Instead he honors a “god of fortresses”—military power—with lavish gifts. His true god is force.

f.g: A god of fortresses or military might.

chapters.n: With this foreign god’s help he attacks strongholds, rewards supporters with rule over many, and parcels out land for profit.

“At the time of the end,” the southern king attacks him, and the northern king storms back with chariots, cavalry, and ships. Many scholars note that verses 40–45 don’t match what is known of Antiochus IV’s last years; many interpreters apply them to the last days.

f.w: at the time of the end

chapters.n: He invades the glorious land and overthrows many countries, but Edom, Moab, and Ammon escape.

f.w: Edom, and Moab, and the chief of the children of Ammon
f.g: Old neighbors of Israel, east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: Egypt will not escape his grasp.
He seizes Egypt’s treasures, with Libya and Cush (Ethiopia) under his control.

f.g: Following him—in submission.

chapters.n: Alarming reports from the east and north drive him out in fury to destroy many.

f.g: News, reports.

chapters.n: He pitches his royal tents between the sea and the holy mountain—yet he comes to his end with no one to help him. However mighty the persecutor, his end is certain.

f.w: between the seas in the glorious holy mountain
f.g: Between the Mediterranean and Mount Zion.

f.w: he shall come to his end, and none shall help him

chapters.n: In the darkest time of trouble ever known, Michael, the great prince who protects Daniel’s people, will arise. Everyone whose name is written in God’s book will be delivered. Latter-day Saints identify Michael as Adam, who will play a key role in the events of the last days.

f.w: a time of trouble, such as never was

chapters.n: One of the clearest Old Testament teachings on resurrection: those who “sleep in the dust” will awake—some to everlasting life, others to shame. Jesus echoed this verse when He taught of the resurrection.

f.w: many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake

f.g: Abhorrence, disgrace.

chapters.n: The wise will shine like the sky, and those who lead others to righteousness will shine like the stars forever. Teaching and helping others toward God has eternal value.

f.w: shine as the brightness of the firmament
they that turn many to righteousness

f.g: The expanse of the sky.

chapters.n: Daniel must seal the book until the time of the end. Then many will travel “to and fro” and knowledge will increase—words many have applied to the explosion of travel, learning, and revealed knowledge in the last days.

f.g: Preserve and secure it, like sealing an important document.

chapters.n: Daniel sees two more heavenly beings, one on each bank of the river.
One asks the man clothed in linen, hovering above the waters, “How long until these astonishing things end?”

Raising both hands to heaven—a doubly solemn oath—he swears by the Eternal One: it will be “a time, times, and half a time,” and when the shattering of the holy people is complete, all will be finished.

f.w: held up his right hand and his left hand unto heaven
a time, times, and an half
f.g: Probably three and a half “times”—a limited period of tribulation.

chapters.n: Daniel honestly admits he doesn’t understand and asks how it will all end. Even prophets don’t always grasp everything they are shown.

f.w: I heard, but I understood not

chapters.n: “Go your way, Daniel.” The words are sealed until the end—their full meaning will be understood later.

f.w: the words are closed up and sealed till the time of the end

chapters.n: Many will be purified and refined through trial, but the wicked will continue in evil and won’t understand. Only the wise will understand—spiritual insight depends on the heart.

f.w: purified, and made white, and tried

chapters.n: From the ending of the daily sacrifice and the setting up of the abomination will be 1,290 days—about three and a half years with an added month.
A blessing for the one who waits patiently and reaches 1,335 days. The varying numbers may mark stages; the main lesson is faithful endurance.

A tender ending for the aged prophet: go your way; you will rest in death, and at the end of days you will rise to receive your allotted inheritance. Daniel’s faithful life ends with the promise of resurrection.

f.w: stand in thy lot at the end of the days
f.g: Rise to receive your inheritance (lot = allotted portion).
